Often, this can be accomplished by developing case studies for sites with a high probability of MTV utilization. PNNL prepared several such studies that were included with the Permitting Plan project deliverable (Section 6, Case Studies). Included case studies corresponded to high commercial interest sites, were aligned with sites used for resource characterizations to inform MTV design criteria, were geographically unique, and represented the types of resources that the MTV is designed to support (river, tidal, ocean current): • Western Passage, Maine • Puget Sound, Washington • Cook Inlet, Alaska • Florida Current, Florida Tactic 4: Secure inaugural MTV use approvals Another tactic to assist MTV users would be securing approvals for specific sites and CECs upon MTV commissioning. If commitments can be obtained from users to use MTV immediately, there may be opportunities to leverage commissioning and/or the DOE NEPA process to at least initiate, but ideally secure, approvals for testing. Commitments would depend upon various factors, including final costs for MTV use, contractual guarantees, available funding, etc. Nonetheless, this tactic could be considered to ensure approval for immediate customer use of the MTV after this project’s completion. 13.4 REGULATORY IMPACT ON MTV DESIGN To inform MTV design efforts, the potential regulatory impact associated with the MTV, CECs it might host, and sites where it might be used were evaluated. 13.4.1 Regulatory Considerations for MTV Regulatory processes that address the safety of marine animals and seabirds from development projects are based on the likely risk to those animals from development. In this case, the risks would be associated with the construction and operation of floating tidal CECs. The construction phase of installing floating tidal turbines is similar to many other in-water projects. It will likely be subject to restrictions based on work windows to protect vulnerable marine species during specific life history stages. The greatest perceived threats to marine animals and birds from the MTV that will influence the regulatory processes may include the items in Table 13-1. The table indicates which aspect of MTV utilization potentially impacts the consideration. Some impacts are dependent upon specific configurations and not always present. For example, if the MTV is supporting a turbine with its structure and no umbilical is needed to transfer power or data, there is no consideration for electromagnetic fields from a power cable. Likewise, if a CEC is deployed fully submerged, it will not present any freeboard for haul-out of marine animals or roosting seabirds. Collision Risk Animals that collide with a rotating turbine blade may suffer recoverable injuries, injuries that later result in their death, or they may be killed outright.
